content_of_post_to_comment:
For years I treated journaling like a mood. If I felt reflective, I wrote. If not, the notebook stayed shut, and every restart felt heavier than the last.

What worked was treating it like an appointment I keep with myself. Every night at the same time I answer the same three questions, and I am done in about five minutes.

What did I do today that is worth remembering? What is one thing that went better than expected? What is the one thing I want to get right tomorrow?

The rules matter more than the questions. I never skip twice in a row. I never edit what I wrote. And I keep the streak visible, because watching a quiet little chain grow turned out to be stronger than any burst of motivation.

Ninety days in, the habit runs itself. If you keep starting and stopping like I did, shrink the session and fix the time. Motivation follows the streak, not the other way around.
comment: I like the rule about never skipping twice, because it makes one missed night feel like a normal lapse instead of the start of another abandoned habit. The visible streak probably helps, but I wonder if the bigger change is removing the daily decision of whether to journal at all. Five minutes at a fixed time leaves very little room for negotiation.
